common_name: Mulgoba Mango (Historic Indian Parent of Haden)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun and well-drained soil; Mulgoba is a historic Indian mango best suited to a warm, frost-free site with ample room to reach its mature size.

directions: Mulgoba is the celebrated Indian mango that USDA plant introduction agents brought to Florida in 1889, with one of the original trees planted on Captain John Haden's Coconut Grove homestead, where a chance seedling from it later became the famous Haden cultivar. The medium-sized, oval fruit ripens to a yellow ground color heavily blushed orange-crimson, enclosing rich, only lightly fibrous flesh long admired among Indian mango connoisseurs for its complex, aromatic sweetness. Like many older Indian cultivars it tends toward alternate bearing and sets fruit most reliably when a dry, sunny bloom period limits anthracnose pressure. Give it excellent drainage and shelter young trees from frost, since mango wood is easily injured by cold below the mid-30s Fahrenheit.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Mango Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Mango Cultivar Notes

common_name: Naga Hai Windmill Palm (Vietnam Dwarf Strain)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens after the soil has warmed following the last frost, in full sun with well-drained soil, and mulch the root zone to buffer temperature swings while the palm establishes.

directions: This compact, slow-growing strain of windmill palm traces to montane collections from northern Vietnam and is prized by collectors for a squatter habit and shorter, broader leaf segments than typical nursery-grown Trachycarpus fortunei. Trunking is much slower than the standard form, so gardeners get a dense, fuller crown for years before appreciable height develops, which suits it to tight courtyards and foundation plantings. Provide the same winter drainage precautions as other windmill palms, since wet, cold soil is the more common threat to survival than the cold itself. Because true stock is uncommon outside specialty palm nurseries, confirm provenance before paying a premium for the name.

common_name: Cinnamon Curls Heuchera (Ruffled Cinnamon-Red Villosa Coral Bells)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; as a villosa selection it tolerates summer heat and humidity better than micrantha-type hybrids and colors up further as nights cool.

directions: Grow in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade, giving afternoon shelter where summers run hot. Cinnamon Curls carries deeply lobed leaves in a warm red-copper cinnamon tone that intensifies as autumn temperatures drop, echoing the seasonal palette of nearby sedums or ornamental kale. Its compact, well-behaved mound suits smaller containers as readily as border edges. Divide every three to four years in spring once the crown becomes congested.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Marvelous Marble Heuchera (Seed-Grown Silver-Veined Native Coral Bells)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or early fall in well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this americana seed strain tolerates deeper shade than many named hybrid coral bells.

directions: Site in well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where this native-species selection is more shade-tolerant than most modern hybrid coral bells. Marvelous Marble emerges purple in spring before settling into deep green marbled with reddish-purple veining and a light silvery overlay, with the pattern shifting through the growing season. Creamy white flowers open earlier than is typical for the genus on comparatively short stems. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; bred in France by Thierry Delabroye and, as a villosa hybrid, notably tolerant of heat and humidity.

directions: Grow in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, keeping foliage out of direct sun to prevent bleaching. Pistache forms a vigorous clump of chartreuse-yellow leaves that deepen to lime green in shadier spots, with a thin red edge developing on the foliage as fall arrives. Airy sprays of cream flowers rise well above the leaves in early summer. Divide every three to four years in spring to maintain a dense, well-colored mound.

common_name: Sparkling Burgundy Heuchera (Glossy Cherry-Maroon Ruffled Coral Bells)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial sun to partial shade; a vigorous, pollinator-attracting older Terra Nova release still widely sold.

directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial sun to partial shade, keeping moisture even in sunnier spots. Sparkling Burgundy holds ruffled six-inch leaves that open bright rose-burgundy in spring, glow cherry to burgundy-red through summer, and deepen to maroon once winter cold sets in. White flowers in spring draw bees and other pollinators to the clump. Divide every three to four years in early spring to keep the mound vigorous.

common_name: Starry Night Heuchera (Near-Black Foliage with Bicolor Flower Spikes)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; a Terra Nova hybrid bred from a dark-leaved seedling crossed with a white-flowered Heuchera sanguinea.

directions: Site in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade for the deepest foliage color. Starry Night holds very dark black-purple leaves year-round on a compact mound, topped in late spring by flower spikes carrying an unusual bicolor mix of white and light pink bells. The strong contrast between near-black foliage and pale flowers makes it a standout even before bloom time. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring.

common_name: Autumn Haze Heuchera (Frosted Purple Foliage with Cinnamon-Pink Overtones)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; semi-evergreen foliage holds interest into winter better than many purple-leaved coral bells.

directions: Grow in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade, allowing more direct light in cooler regions to intensify color. Autumn Haze combines pink, cinnamon, and purple tones across a frosted purple leaf base, giving the mound a hazy, ever-shifting appearance that persists into winter on its semi-evergreen foliage. Rose-tinted flowers rise well above the clump on tall stems in spring. Divide every three to four years in spring once the crown becomes crowded.

common_name: Fandango Heuchera (Veiled-Metallic Ruffled Coral Bells with Coral Wand Flowers)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in part shade to full sun; a compact, repeat-blooming Terra Nova release grown as much for flowers as foliage.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in part shade to full sun, deadheading spent stalks to encourage repeat flushes of bloom. Fandango stays compact and free-flowering, its ruffled leaves carrying a shimmering, veiled-metallic sheen beneath wand-like stalks of coral flowers that rebloom through the growing season. The short flower stems keep the display from flopping even in a modest-sized planting. Divide every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor and bloom count.

common_name: Velvet Night Heuchera (Plush Slate-Black Foliage with Metallic Purple Overlay)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade, with consistent moisture if grown in more sun; a micrantha x americana Terra Nova hybrid.

directions: Site in moist, well-drained soil in part shade for the richest color and softest leaf texture, since the shimmering overlay shows best out of hot direct sun. Velvet Night forms a low mound of plush, slate-black leaves with a complex metallic purple sheen that feels velvety to the touch, a hybrid between Heuchera micrantha and Heuchera americana. Greenish-white bell flowers open on wiry stems in late spring and early summer. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring.

common_name: Galaxy Heuchera (Hot-Pink Speckled Variegated Coral Bells)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in part shade to full sun; a heat- and cold-tolerant Terra Nova variegated release.

directions: Grow in well-drained, humus-rich soil in part shade to full sun, where strong light intensifies the variegated pattern. Galaxy opens with startling bright red leaves that darken with age while heavy speckling of hot pink against a near-black background becomes more pronounced through the season, resembling a field of stars. White flowers appear in summer above the leathery foliage. Divide every three to four years in spring to keep the pattern crisp and the clump vigorous.

common_name: Changeling Heuchera (Weekly Color-Shifting Peach-to-Champagne Coral Bells)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; a low, wide-spreading Terra Nova hybrid grown for its shifting multi-tone foliage.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade, where the low, wide mound has room to spread beyond its height. Changeling earns its name from heavily veined leaves that shift color roughly every week, opening in peach and cherry tones before moving through champagne to green, all touched with a light silver cast, so the clump often shows several colors at once. White flowers appear on wiry stems in early summer but are secondary to the foliage show. Divide every three to four years in spring once the crown becomes congested.

common_name: Iridescent Heuchera (Pearly Lavender-Rose Foliage Coral Bells)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; an unusually sun-tolerant, vigorous Terra Nova pastel-foliage release.

directions: Site in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Iridescent tolerates more direct sun than most pastel-leaved coral bells without losing color. The tight mound of pearly foliage opens rose-pink and gradually shifts to a soft silver-lavender as the season progresses, a color combination uncommon among heuchera introductions. Light pink flowers echo the soft leaf tones in late spring. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to keep the mound full.

common_name: Fireworks Heuchera (Bronze Foliage with Explosive Coral Flower Display)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in part shade to full sun; grown primarily as a long-season pollinator-friendly bloomer rather than a foliage specimen.

directions: Grow in well-drained, humus-rich soil in part shade to full sun, where at least a few hours of direct light keeps the bloom count high. Fireworks bears a lightly ruffled bronze foliage mound but is prized chiefly for its wiry stems loaded with small coral bell-shaped flowers that open in a prolonged, explosive-looking display from May into August. The long bloom season reliably attracts hummingbirds and butterflies. Divide every three to four years in spring to maintain flowering vigor.

common_name: Copper Cascade Heucherella (Trailing Rust-Resistant Copper-Gold Foamy Bells)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; part of Terra Nova's rust-resistant Cascade series bred with a smaller, tighter trailing habit than older heucherella lines.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, letting the stems trail rather than confining them against upright neighbors. Copper Cascade produces a mound of rosy copper-gold leaves veiled in pink with fine burgundy veining, rooting along its trailing stems as it spreads, and holds up notably well against the leaf rust that troubles older heucherella cultivars. Sprays of creamy white flowers rise on slender stems in late spring. Its compact, cascading habit suits raised containers and the edges of shaded retaining walls.

common_name: Hopscotch Heucherella (Fun and Games Series Orange-to-Bronze Lacy Foamy Bells)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; part of the Walters Gardens Fun and Games heucherella series marketed for heat and humidity tolerance.

directions: Grow in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, watering during dry spells to keep the finely lobed foliage from wilting. Hopscotch opens in early spring with vivid red leaves and deep red centers, mellows to bronze-red through the season, and settles into deep green by summer, giving each mound a distinctly lacy, finely cut texture. Creamy bottlebrush-shaped flowers appear above the foliage in late spring. Divide congested clumps every three years to keep the mound full and well colored.
